headline: A key that cannot sign for itself can still prove possession, by answering the authority's encrypted challenge.
summary:
A certification request normally proves the client holds the private key by signing with it. A key agreement key cannot sign, so RFC 5272 gives the authority another way: it encrypts a proof value to the key being certified and asks the client to return a MAC computed with it. Until now pki.cmc surfaced that challenge as unread bytes, so a client enrolling such a key had to decode the control, decrypt the value, check it and compute the answer itself.

pki.cmc.build takes opts popChallenge and does all four, and pki.schema.cmc reads both controls of the exchange. The check the RFC makes mandatory is not optional here: the answer is produced only by the path that confirms the decrypted value is the one the authority issued.

Added: pki.schema.cmc.parse decodes the two controls of the challenge-response proof of possession (RFC 5272 section 6.7). An Encrypted POP control surfaces as encryptedPOP with its request, its enveloped challenge, the two algorithm identifiers and the witness; a Decrypted POP control surfaces as decryptedPOP with its body part, algorithm and proof. The enveloped challenge is surfaced as the bytes it arrived as, since it is opened with key material the parser does not hold. Both algorithm identifiers keep their parameters, so a client answers with what it was sent. A control of either kind that is not the structure the section defines is refused with cmc/bad-pop-challenge. The two travel in opposite directions, so an Encrypted POP in a request or a Decrypted POP in a response is refused with cmc/control-misplaced. The challenge is held to what a client would have to answer: its envelope to the CMS EnvelopedData definition, and the request it quotes to the definition of the arm it uses, so a challenge nothing could answer is refused rather than surfaced as one.

pki.cmc.build(spec, signer) takes spec popChallenge of { challenge, recipient } and answers it: the enveloped proof value is decrypted with the recipient key material, hashed under the witness algorithm the challenge names, and compared with the witness it carries. A value that does not decrypt, or that does not hash to that witness, is not the value the authority issued, so the request is refused with cmc/pop-failed and no proof is sent. The section makes that abort mandatory, and answering is not separable from checking: pki.cmc.build computes a proof only after the witness matches. A Decrypted POP control hand-encoded into spec.controls alongside spec popChallenge is refused, since a message carrying two leaves the authority no proof to check; the same now holds for the Identity Proof and POP Link controls that spec identityProof and spec popLink compute.

The answer is a MAC over the request the challenge carried, keyed by the decrypted proof value, under the algorithm the challenge named rather than one the client picks. A proof value longer than 64 bytes is truncated to 64 for the key, which the section states and an implementation that skips it will compute a different proof than the authority expects. The control names the certification request in the new request, so a request carrying more than one is refused rather than guessed at. RFC 5274 section 4.2 sets what a conforming client answers under: SHA-1 or SHA-256 for the witness, HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-SHA256 for the proof. Anything else is refused rather than defaulted. The decrypted proof value and the key derived from it are wiped once the answer is built.

A PKCS#10 request whose signature algorithm is id-alg-noSignature is accepted when this message answers a challenge for that same request. A decrypt-only key cannot sign the request that asks for its certificate, and RFC 5272 Appendix C.1 fills the signature field with an algorithm that proves nothing and sends the proof through the section 6.7 challenge instead; the request was previously refused with cmc/bad-popo, so the enrollment the challenge exists for could not be made. The challenge has to prove the key the request asks for: section 6.7 encrypts the proof value to that key, so the request is accepted only when the key that opened the challenge is the request's own subject public key. A challenge opened by any other key, or by a password or a key-encryption key, says nothing about the key being certified and does not stand in for the missing signature. The two keys are compared as keys rather than as encodings, so a curve point written in compressed form matches the same point written uncompressed. A key whose public half cannot be derived on the running Node, which today means the composite ML-KEM families, leaves the request refused rather than accepted. Without an answered challenge for that request it is still refused, since it carries no proof of possession at all, and its parameters must be present and encoded as NULL. A request that does carry a signature is still held to it.
pki.schema.cmc.parse also reports how many recipients the challenge names, as encryptedPOP cmsRecipientCount, so a client answering one knows how many to try without walking the envelope itself.

The client decrypts with the key alone, which is what the exchange requires: the key being certified has no certificate for a recipient identifier to name. Section 6.7 says the identifier should be the request's subject key identifier, and that form is answered. The alternative it allows, an issuer and serial number whose issuer is encoded as NULL, is not: that is not a Name, and the CMS EnvelopedData definition refuses it. A challenge addressed only that way is refused while parsing, with cmc/bad-pop-challenge naming the reason, and pki.cms.decrypt could not have opened it either. The proof also has to cover the request the message carries: a challenge quoting a different certification request is refused rather than answered for the wrong one.
Fixed: pki.cms.decrypt opens a key-agreement recipient whose encrypted key is not the first one listed. One KeyAgreeRecipientInfo can carry an encrypted key for several recipients under a single originator, and a caller decrypting with a private key alone has no recipient identifier to select its own entry by, so only the first entry was tried and a message addressed to that caller was refused as undecryptable. A caller with no certificate is now offered every entry, and AES key wrap's integrity check settles which one belongs to the key, so an entry opens only for the key it was encrypted to. A caller that supplies a certificate is unaffected: its entry is still chosen by recipient identifier. At most 64 entries are tried, since the list arrives with the message; a longer list still opens on an entry within that bound, and one whose only openable entry sits past it is refused with cms/too-many-recipient-keys.

pki.schema.cms.parse refuses a key-agreement recipient that names no encrypted key. Such a recipient names nobody, so nothing could open the content it is attached to; it now fails with cms/bad-recipient-encrypted-keys while parsing rather than reaching a decrypt that has nothing to try.

pki.cms.decrypt takes the curve of a key-agreement originator that omitted its parameters from the recipient's own private key. RFC 5753 section 7.1 allows the originator to omit them because the recipient knows the curve, but the curve was read only from a recipient certificate, so a caller decrypting with a key alone was refused with cms/unsupported-algorithm.
